quizzes.title: Ethics Comprehensive Quiz
quizzes.description: A continuous review of five Ethics themes.
quizzes.subject: Ethics

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: Which etymology and definition are paired correctly?

choices.text: Ethos means wisdom; ethics is love of learning
Philos means love and sophia means wisdom; philosophy is love of wisdom
Mores means character; morality is a public law
Sophia means custom; morals are philosophical questions

questions.explanation: The notes derive philosophy from philos, love, and sophia, wisdom.

distractorExplanations.a: ** A assigns the wrong meanings.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C reverses ethos and mores and changes morality into law.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D assigns the wrong meaning to sophia.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: How do the notes distinguish ethics from morals?

choices.text: Ethics studies the morality of acts, while morals are conduct standards rooted in mores or customs
Ethics is subjective feeling, while morals are laws enacted by the state
Ethics concerns physics, while morals concern aesthetics
Ethics is personal custom, while morals reject conduct standards

questions.explanation: Ethics is presented as the study of the morality of acts; morals are standards people are encouraged to observe.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B confuses morality with state law.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C assigns unrelated fields.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D contradicts the definition of morals.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: Morality is described as a personal compass of right and wrong and therefore has a subjective dimension.
questions.explanation: The notes place morality within the person as a personal compass.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: Which feature makes a standard moral rather than merely popular?

choices.text: Its validity rests on reason and impartial consideration
It reflects the preference of the largest group
It benefits the decision-maker before everyone else
It changes whenever immediate feelings change

questions.explanation: Moral standards rest on reason, impartiality, and universalizability rather than popularity.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B substitutes majority approval for reason.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C privileges self-interest rather than impartiality.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D makes morality depend on unstable feelings.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: What does universalizability require in the notes?

choices.text: The standard should be good for everyone, not just the actor
The standard should be accepted only by experts
The standard should benefit one organization first
The standard should follow whatever is culturally popular

questions.explanation: Universalizability asks whether the standard can apply beyond one favored person.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B limits the audience without basis.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C conflicts with impartiality.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D confuses popularity with moral validity.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: Why are moral standards preferred over self-interest and other values?

choices.text: They concern significant benefit or injury and require impartial reasons
They guarantee immediate comfort for the actor
They eliminate emotions from every decision
They are valid whenever they are widely repeated

questions.explanation: The notes give moral standards priority because they concern human welfare and impartial justification.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B centers comfort and self-interest.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C ignores the legitimate role of feeling.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D mistakes repetition for validity.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: What is the proper relationship between reason and feelings in a moral act?

choices.text: Reason tempers immediate impulses, while feeling helps make decisions humane
Feeling must replace reason whenever empathy is present
Reason should apply rules without regard for the other person
Reason and feeling cannot contribute to the same decision

questions.explanation: The notes require both: reason checks compulsion and feeling supplies humane empathy.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B makes feeling sufficient by itself.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C describes reason blinded by strict rules.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D rejects the complementary relationship.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: Empathy is treated as necessarily irrational and therefore excluded from moral action.
questions.explanation: The notes expressly present feeling and empathy as part of humane moral decision-making.
questions.correctedStatement: Empathy is not inherently irrational; moral action integrates humane feeling with reason.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: A manager follows a rule mechanically even though its application harms a vulnerable person. Which danger from the notes is illustrated?

choices.text: Reason becoming blind through rigid rule-following
Feelings seeking immediate fulfillment
Universalizability correcting self-interest
Impartiality forbidding arbitrary treatment

questions.explanation: Reason can become incapable of empathy when it rigidly implements its own rules.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B describes impulsive feeling, not mechanical rationalism.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C and D are safeguards rather than the danger.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B describes impulsive feeling, not mechanical rationalism.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: Who is the moral agent?

choices.text: The person whose human acts flow from personhood
The organization that supplies every personal value
The audience that approves an action
The rule that determines conduct without a person

questions.explanation: The notes identify the person - you - as the moral agent.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B may influence but is not the personal agent.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C approval does not create agency.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D rules do not act by themselves.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: What do the notes mean by saying human acts determine the person?

choices.text: Actions express and help form who the person is
Actions have no relationship to character
Only thoughts, not acts, reveal personhood
A bad decision harms others but never the actor

questions.explanation: Human acts flow from personhood and express the actor's developing character.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B and C deny the stated connection.
distractorExplanations.c: ** D contradicts the claim that the agent is the first victim of wrongdoing.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B and C deny the stated connection.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Ethics
questions.prompt: The moral agent may be the first victim of a bad decision because wrongdoing also damages the kind of person the agent becomes.
questions.explanation: The notes explicitly identify the agent as the first victim of a wrong action.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: Which set lists the three levels of moral dilemma in the notes?

choices.text: Individual, organizational, and systemic or structural
Personal, legal, and international
Emotional, rational, and spiritual
Private, public, and religious

questions.explanation: The material distinguishes dilemmas by individual, organizational, and systemic or structural level.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B, C, and D use categories not listed.
distractorExplanations.c: ** B, C, and D use categories not listed.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B, C, and D use categories not listed.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: What conflict best characterizes an organizational dilemma?

choices.text: Individual needs versus the collective purpose of the organization
One sense pleasure versus another sense pleasure
A private feeling versus a physical law
A present fact versus an unchangeable past

questions.explanation: Organizational dilemmas arise within a sector or institution when personal needs and collective purposes conflict.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B concerns sensory preference.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C and D are not the organizational contrast given.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B concerns sensory preference.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: Why are systemic or structural dilemmas especially difficult?

choices.text: They involve enduring trade-offs in an ongoing search for a satisfactory system
They always have one obvious answer known in advance
They concern only one person's temporary preference
They disappear when managers follow popular opinion

questions.explanation: Structural dilemmas may persist without clean solutions and require navigating trade-offs.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B denies their open-ended character.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C describes an individual issue.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D substitutes popularity for reasoning.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: A moral judgment is primarily a matter of personal taste whenever the decision is difficult.
questions.explanation: The notes state that moral judgment requires reason rather than mere preferences or tastes.
questions.correctedStatement: Difficulty does not convert moral judgment into taste; relevant facts, interests, actions, and consequences must be reasoned through.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: What is the first step in the moral-reasoning process given?

choices.text: Identify the morally relevant aspects as comprehensively as possible
Choose the action with the most immediate benefit
Ask which option is personally comfortable
Decide first, then gather only supporting facts

questions.explanation: Sound reasoning begins by identifying the morally relevant features of the situation.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B and C privilege convenience.
distractorExplanations.c: ** D reverses inquiry and invites confirmation bias.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B and C privilege convenience.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: After identifying morally relevant aspects, what should the agent do next?

choices.text: Weigh their significance while considering affected persons' views of benefit and harm
Ignore individual perspectives to remain neutral
Count how many people prefer each option
Apply the strictest rule without context

questions.explanation: The second step weighs significance and gives due importance to concerned persons' understandings of benefit and harm.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B mistakes impartiality for ignoring persons.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C equates popularity with morality.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D bypasses the stated evaluation.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: Which step directly prevents the agent from treating the dilemma as a choice between only two assumed options?

choices.text: Identify all possible actions and their likely consequences
Focus only on the actor's first impulse
Accept the organization's usual practice
Delay the decision until everyone agrees

questions.explanation: Comprehensive option-generation reveals alternatives and foreseeable effects.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B narrows inquiry.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C treats custom as decisive.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D makes unanimity a requirement not stated.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: What is the final step of moral reasoning in the notes?

choices.text: Integrate the elements and choose the action most ethically justified by reason
Select the action that produces the strongest emotion
Follow the option favored by the most powerful stakeholder
Avoid action whenever consequences are uncertain

questions.explanation: The agent considers the full analysis and decides which action reason supports as most ethically justified.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B substitutes emotion for justification.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C violates impartiality.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D treats uncertainty as a bar to responsible choice.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: What does impartiality require?

choices.text: Each affected person's welfare must count as equally important
The actor's welfare must count more because the actor decides
All people must receive identical outcomes in every case
No one may consider the concrete facts of a person's situation

questions.explanation: Impartiality forbids arbitrariness and gives equal moral importance to each person's interests.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B privileges the actor.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C confuses equal consideration with identical outcomes.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D removes relevant context.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: Which behavior belongs to a conscientious moral agent?

choices.text: Sifting facts and examining their implications before accepting principles
Accepting any rule that benefits the agent
Ignoring affected persons to remain detached
Treating familiar principles as sound without scrutiny

questions.explanation: The conscientious agent investigates facts, considers everyone impartially, and scrutinizes principles.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B violates impartiality.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C confuses detachment with fairness.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D rejects scrutiny.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: Impartiality forbids arbitrary favoritism but does not require ignoring differences that are morally relevant.
questions.explanation: Equal importance of welfare is compatible with careful attention to relevant facts and harms.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Moral Dilemmas and the Minimum Requirements of Morality
questions.prompt: Which two claims summarize the nature of morality in the notes?

choices.text: Judgments need good reasons, and each person's interests require impartial consideration
Judgments need strong feelings, and the actor's interests come first
Judgments need public approval, and organizations determine value
Judgments need legal enforcement, and customs settle every conflict

questions.explanation: The notes conclude with reason-giving and impartial regard for each person.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B, C, and D substitute emotion, popularity, authority, or custom for the stated requirements.
distractorExplanations.c: ** B, C, and D substitute emotion, popularity, authority, or custom for the stated requirements.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B, C, and D substitute emotion, popularity, authority, or custom for the stated requirements.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: Why is freedom necessary for ethics according to the notes?

choices.text: Responsibility, praise, and blame presuppose that people can choose
Ethics requires people to act without any limits
Freedom guarantees every choice is morally good
Responsibility exists only when consequences are pleasant

questions.explanation: Without meaningful freedom, accountability for action loses its basis.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B confuses freedom with absence of structure.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C mistakes choosing for choosing well.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D makes accountability depend on comfort.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: What is described as the object of the will?

choices.text: The good as the person perceives some benefit in it
Whatever causes the greatest pain
A value imposed without any perceived benefit
The past considered as unchangeable

questions.explanation: The will tends toward what appears good or beneficial to the person.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B and C contradict the orientation toward perceived good.
distractorExplanations.c: ** D concerns historicity, not the object of will.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B and C contradict the orientation toward perceived good.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: How can deception affect freedom and accountability?

choices.text: Ignorance caused by deception can nullify informed choice and reduce blame
Deception increases freedom by adding possibilities
A deceived victim is fully responsible for the deceiver's falsehood
False information respects freedom because the person still acts

questions.explanation: Choice is not fully free when crucial knowledge is withheld or falsified.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B mistakes misinformation for opportunity.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C shifts blame to the victim.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D ignores the need for informed agency.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: Which pair belongs to reflective analysis as a way of exercising freedom?

choices.text: Self-possession and freedom of choice through questioning, distance, and valuing
Reinforcement and automatic response
Popularity and conformity
Punishment and environmental control

questions.explanation: The notes emphasize owning oneself and critically distancing from influences.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B and D describe deterministic conditioning.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C suppresses reflective independence.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B and D describe deterministic conditioning.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: What is B. F. Skinner's total determinism said to claim?

choices.text: Behavior is molded through reinforcement rather than genuinely free choice
People are structureless and create themselves without influence
Values are eternal objects independent of bearers
Dialogue exists only between fully autonomous institutions

questions.explanation: The Skinner section reduces apparent freedom to conditioning and reinforcement.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B describes Sartrean absolute freedom.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C describes Scheler's value theory.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D is unrelated to the determinism account.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: Which group is identified as structures influencing choice?

choices.text: Genetic, biological, physical, environmental, and cultural factors
Only legal commands and court decisions
Only conscious plans chosen by the person
Values that never interact with embodiment or history

questions.explanation: The notes recognize bodily, developmental, cultural, and external constraints.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is too narrow.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C ignores unchosen structures.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D denies historical and embodied influence.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: What is surface freedom?

choices.text: The felt ability to do what one wants without asking whether the wanting is controlled
The complete absence of causal influence
The disciplined questioning of inherited structures
The capacity to create values independent of every condition

questions.explanation: Surface freedom stops at acting on desire and does not examine how desire was formed.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B and D describe unrealistic absolute independence.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C is reflective or structured freedom.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B and D describe unrealistic absolute independence.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: Which example best fits sociological determinism?

choices.text: Explaining misconduct through media, abuse, cultural mores, or social disorder
Claiming urgent hunger predetermines theft
Claiming divine foreknowledge fixes every choice
Claiming values are independent of their carriers

questions.explanation: Sociological determinism locates behavioral causes in society and culture.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is psychological determinism in the notes.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C is theological determinism.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D concerns Scheler.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: What problem does theological determinism raise?

choices.text: Divine omniscience appears to conflict with human free will
Physical disability limits a chosen occupation
Urgent needs appear to predetermine action
Culture creates needs through external forces

questions.explanation: If every choice and consequence is already known, the notes ask how free will can remain.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is a physical limitation.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C is psychological determinism.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D is environmental or sociological influence.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: What is psychological determinism in the notes?

choices.text: The belief that action is predetermined by the most urgent need
The belief that society alone creates all wrongdoing
The belief that God has no knowledge of choices
The belief that persons are completely structureless

questions.explanation: The example is stealing under poverty or extreme hunger because the urgent need controls action.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is sociological determinism.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C misstates the theological issue.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D describes Sartre more closely.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: Historicity means people cannot question, resist, or gain distance from inherited environmental structures.
questions.explanation: The notes say the past is unchangeable, but a person can question, hesitate, challenge, and revolt against structures.
questions.correctedStatement: Historicity conditions the person, yet reflective distance permits resistance and new choices.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: How does Sartre oppose determinism?

choices.text: Existence involves questioning and resistance, and the person remains responsible for choices
A person's past fixes identity permanently
Structures remove responsibility for consequences
Freedom is possible only after a fixed essence is completed

questions.explanation: Sartre treats human being and freedom as inseparable and rejects a predetermined identity.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B contradicts freedom from the past.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C denies Sartrean responsibility.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D reverses existence and freedom.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: Why can freedom produce anxiety?

choices.text: Choosing one possibility excludes countless others and leaves the chooser responsible
Freedom permits every possibility to be realized at once
Anxiety proves that choices have no consequences
Structures decide, so the person never truly chooses

questions.explanation: Finite choice condemns other possibilities to non-being and cannot escape consequence.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B denies exclusivity of choice.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C denies responsibility.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D states determinism rather than anxiety of freedom.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Man and Freedom
questions.prompt: What is structured freedom?

choices.text: Freedom exercised within historicity and structures that can be questioned, accepted, or transformed
Complete conditioning with no reflective distance
Structureless choice untouched by body, culture, or past
Obedience to every offering of the world

questions.explanation: Structured freedom integrates real influences with the capacity to respond and build a life project.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B removes freedom.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C removes structure.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D denies selective response.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: Where do values originate in Scheler's account as presented?

choices.text: In pre-rational preferring grounded in an ordo amoris
In majority vote after rational calculation
In the physical bearer that temporarily carries them
In legal rules that define what people must value

questions.explanation: Values are disclosed through a pre-rational logic of the heart or ordo amoris.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B makes value a product of popularity.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C confuses value with its changeable bearer.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D reduces value to law.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: Because values are a priori, they are objective and not created by the changing goods that bear them.
questions.explanation: The notes emphasize the objectivity, immutability, and independence of values.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: Which example best illustrates the independence of value from its bearer?

choices.text: Friendship remains a value even when a particular friend betrays someone
Bread has value only when one person owns the entire loaf
Health ceases to be valuable when a person neglects it
Beauty exists only while one observer happens to feel pleasure

questions.explanation: The bearer may fail or change while the value-quality remains.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B concerns divisibility of a sensory good.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C contradicts health's independence from striving.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D reduces objective value to a feeling-state.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: Which statement about positive and negative values is correct?

choices.text: A value cannot be positive and negative at the same time
Every value becomes positive when strongly desired
The non-existence of a positive value is itself positive
The existence of a negative value is itself positive

questions.explanation: Scheler's ordered realm distinguishes positive and negative values consistently.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B makes desire decisive.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C and D reverse the stated polarity.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B makes desire decisive.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: What is the hierarchy from lowest to highest?

choices.text: Sensory, vital, spiritual, holy or unholy
Vital, sensory, holy, spiritual
Spiritual, sensory, vital, holy
Holy, spiritual, vital, sensory

questions.explanation: The notes rank sensory lowest, then vital, spiritual, and the holy highest.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B and C scramble the middle ranks.
distractorExplanations.c: ** D reverses the hierarchy.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B and C scramble the middle ranks.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: Which value belongs to the sensory level?

choices.text: Pleasant versus unpleasant
Noble versus vulgar
Just versus unjust
Holy versus unholy

questions.explanation: Sensory values concern agreeable or disagreeable experience and pleasure or pain.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is vital.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C is spiritual.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D is the highest modality.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: Which description fits vital values?

choices.text: Health, sickness, vigor, exhaustion, courage, and anxiety connected with life
Beauty, justice, and pure knowledge independent of body
Faith, awe, bliss, and despair directed to absolute objects
Technical luxury measured only by immediate pleasure

questions.explanation: Vital values concern well-being, the noble and vulgar, and life-toned states.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B describes spiritual values.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C describes holy values.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D belongs under sensory values.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: Which set consists of spiritual values?

choices.text: Beauty and ugliness, justice and injustice, and pure knowledge
Pleasure and pain, luxury and technical convenience
Health and sickness, vigor and exhaustion
Bliss and despair, faith and adoration

questions.explanation: Spiritual values include aesthetic, juridical, and pure-knowledge values.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is sensory.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C is vital.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D corresponds to holy and unholy.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: What distinguishes holy and unholy values?

choices.text: They appear in relation to absolute objects and exceed dependence on particular holy persons or things
They concern bodily health and general well-being
They are measured by how many people divide a material good
They consist solely in artistic beauty and scientific knowledge

questions.explanation: The highest modality concerns the absolute sphere, with responses such as faith, awe, bliss, or despair.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is vital.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C concerns divisibility.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D is spiritual.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: Which principle explains why a work of art may rank above a loaf of bread in the relevant comparison?

choices.text: Higher values are less divisible among carriers or participants
Higher values produce stronger bodily pleasure
Higher values must belong to fewer people
Higher values depend more heavily on material objects

questions.explanation: Countless people can appreciate art without dividing and exhausting it as they would a loaf.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B reduces rank to sensory intensity.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C mistakes less divisibility for exclusivity.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D states the opposite tendency.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: How does depth of fulfillment relate to value height?

choices.text: Higher values bring deeper contentment rather than repeated search for more enjoyment
Lower sensory values always provide the deepest completion
Value height is unrelated to satisfaction
Only the number of carriers determines depth

questions.explanation: Scheler links higher rank with deeper fulfillment; sensory enjoyment tends to seek further enjoyment.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B reverses the hierarchy.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C denies one of the five principles.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D reduces rank to one different criterion.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: Where are moral good and evil located in Scheler's account?

choices.text: In the person's act of realizing higher or lower, positive or negative values
As a fifth value modality beside the holy
Inside goods regardless of any acting person
In pleasure whenever the actor feels satisfied

questions.explanation: Good and evil ride on the deed; only persons originally bear moral value through preferring and acting.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B the notes exclude them from the four modalities.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C goods are not original moral agents.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D confuses satisfaction with moral rank.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: Choosing a lower or negative value over an available higher or positive value is described as morally good.
questions.explanation: The notes call realization of the higher or positive good and realization of the lower or negative evil.
questions.correctedStatement: Moral goodness follows the loving preference and realization of higher and positive values.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Max Scheler and the Hierarchy of Values
questions.prompt: What is a person's moral tenor?

choices.text: The operative ordo amoris directing willing and preference toward higher or lower values
The temporary feeling produced by one pleasant object
The legal status assigned by an organization
The physical strength of the value bearer

questions.explanation: Moral tenor is the person's underlying system of valuations and value-preferences.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is too episodic and sensory.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C and D are unrelated to the personal order of love.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B is too episodic and sensory.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: What is the shared thesis attributed to Buber and Dy?

choices.text: Human fulfillment arises through relationships that encounter persons as unique subjects rather than objects or instruments
Collective membership automatically creates genuine personal relationship
Love is identical with attraction, compatibility, or need satisfaction
Dialogue is the sum of two private psychological states

questions.explanation: Both accounts center authentic encounter with a unique person.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B confuses the social with the interhuman.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C reduces love to accompanying features.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D denies the reality that arises between persons.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: What is the interhuman?

choices.text: The living reality arising between persons who genuinely turn toward one another
The private inner state of one isolated individual
Any group identity that suppresses personal feeling
A technique for producing agreement through influence

questions.explanation: The interhuman exists in the between of genuine personal encounter.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B locates it entirely within one psyche.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C describes collective life without recognition.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D may become manipulation rather than dialogue.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: Which three conditions support the interhuman in the summary?

choices.text: Truthful being, making the other present, and freedom from imposition
Popularity, uniformity, and obedience
Attraction, possession, and reciprocity
Analysis, classification, and prediction alone

questions.explanation: Authenticity, personal presence, and non-domination structure genuine relation.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B describes conformity.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C misstates love as possession.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D reduces a person to information.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: What is “seeming” in Buber's contrast?

choices.text: Constructing an image to produce a desired impression
Speaking spontaneously from what one is
Performing any dramatic role or childhood imitation
Withholding every private thought from another person

questions.explanation: Seeming places a manufactured identity between persons.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B describes being.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C can be legitimate performance without existential deception.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D honesty does not require total disclosure.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: Authentic being requires unrestricted confession of every thought and feeling.
questions.explanation: The text distinguishes honesty from total disclosure; the requirement is not to let a fabricated identity stand in one's place.
questions.correctedStatement: Being means truthful presence without manipulative self-fabrication, not disclosure without boundaries.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: What does confirmation of another person mean?

choices.text: Recognizing the person's real existence and standing as a partner without necessarily approving the belief
Agreeing with every conviction the person holds
Refusing to judge any harmful action
Reducing the person to a predictable type

questions.explanation: Confirmation permits strict opposition while affirming the bearer of the conviction.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B confuses affirmation with agreement.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C turns respect into moral indifference.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D is inadequate perception.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: What is personal making present?

choices.text: A disciplined effort to apprehend the other as a whole, unique, developing person
A fantasy that projects one's own experience onto the other
A file of facts that fully reduces the person to a category
An agreement to avoid all disagreement

questions.explanation: It involves imagining the real situation of this person without claiming it as one's own.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is projection rather than presence.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C is reductive analysis.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D is unnecessary for genuine dialogue.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: How does unfolding differ from imposition?

choices.text: Unfolding helps possibilities within the other become actual; imposition installs an identity or conclusion originating in oneself
Unfolding secures obedience; imposition develops judgment
Unfolding ignores the other's freedom; imposition protects it
They are two names for the same influence process

questions.explanation: The ethical distinction turns on whether the other's own freedom participates in development.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B and C reverse the concepts.
distractorExplanations.c: ** D erases the central contrast.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B and C reverse the concepts.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: Why is propaganda the mastery of imposition?

choices.text: It uses knowledge of people to bypass judgment and treats success as a matter of how many are moved
It invites answers capable of changing the situation
It gradually increases the learner's independent judgment
It accepts the other as a unique partner rather than an audience

questions.explanation: Propaganda controls appearance and response while preserving an illusion of autonomy.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B and D describe dialogue.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C describes education as unfolding.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B and D describe dialogue.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: What is the appeal of the other in Dy's account?

choices.text: The vulnerable and free person whose existence interrupts self-absorption
A spoken request that must be granted exactly as stated
A set of attractive qualities that satisfy the lover's needs
An abstract category called humanity without concrete persons

questions.explanation: The appeal is the person, not merely a request or collection of qualities.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B can confuse love with compliance.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C reduces the person to traits and need satisfaction.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D lacks concrete encounter.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: What response is appropriate if the appeal of the other is the person?

choices.text: The gift of oneself through committed presence and fitting action
Possession of the other's future choices
Advice given without listening
Material assistance as a complete substitute for presence

questions.explanation: Dy answers person with person: the self becomes present through appropriate concrete care.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B violates freedom.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C bypasses encounter.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D reduces the response to one possible service.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: Why are respect and patience necessary to love?

choices.text: They prevent care from becoming domination and honor the other's rhythm of development
They guarantee the other will reciprocate
They allow the lover to choose the other's identity
They remove the need for concrete action

questions.explanation: Love wills the other's free self-realization rather than imposing a timetable or plan.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B makes return the controlling motive.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C contradicts otherness.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D detaches love from embodied history.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: What does the “we” created by reciprocal love mean?

choices.text: A shared history and world in which two become one while remaining distinct
A third entity that owns and dissolves the individuals
Complete agreement on every belief and action
Dependence that ends independent thought and responsibility

questions.explanation: The we is unity without assimilation, built through shared practices and possibilities.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B erases persons.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C makes uniformity necessary.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D describes unhealthy absorption.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: Why is love described as historical?

choices.text: It develops with a particular embodied person through concrete events and remembered actions
It is an abstract feeling toward humanity alone
It exists independently of any story or action
It is identical with admiration from a distance

questions.explanation: Waiting, listening, protecting, remembering, and forgiving give a relationship its history.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B avoids the concrete person.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C removes lived development.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D lacks shared history and encounter.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: Which criticism targets personal making present?

choices.text: People may overestimate their ability to grasp another as a whole, so understanding should remain humble and revisable
It pays too much attention to institutional power
It proves every dialogue is impossible
It requires agreement with the other's convictions

questions.explanation: Bias, projection, trauma, and self-deception make interpersonal understanding fragile.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is a different criticism of the face-to-face focus.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C is stronger than the critique.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D contradicts confirmation without approval.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: What limitation arises when the framework is applied to employer-employee or abuser-victim relationships?

choices.text: Unequal power and coercion may block genuine reciprocity despite sincere speech
The parties necessarily have identical freedom
Face-to-face dialogue automatically removes economic dependence
Institutional conditions never affect personal encounter

questions.explanation: The critique says law, hierarchy, dependence, and coercion cannot be reduced to mutual presence.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B, C, and D deny the structural problem.
distractorExplanations.c: ** B, C, and D deny the structural problem.
distractorExplanations.d: ** B, C, and D deny the structural problem.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: What practical correction is suggested for the imposition-education contrast?

choices.text: Make authority accountable, limited, transparent, and increasingly participatory
Eliminate all guidance, curricula, rules, and judgment
Permit educators to impose any end they sincerely believe is good
Measure education only by how many students comply

questions.explanation: Some authority is unavoidable; the ethical task is to structure it toward participation and judgment.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is impractical and not the proposed correction.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C makes sincerity sufficient.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D reproduces propaganda's quantitative focus.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: Why is Dy's rhetoric of total, eternal love criticized?

choices.text: Healthy love may require boundaries, distance, or separation when a relationship is dangerous
Love never includes trust or commitment
Reciprocal relationships cannot form a shared world
Patience makes all boundaries unnecessary

questions.explanation: Respect and freedom sometimes require limits rather than limitless devotion.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B rejects too much.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C denies the creative we.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D turns patience into submission.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: The strongest practical test of a healthy “we” is that each participant becomes less capable of independent judgment.
questions.explanation: The conclusion says healthy relationship should make each person more capable of thought, choice, and responsibility.
questions.correctedStatement: A healthy we deepens connection while strengthening each participant's freedom and responsibility.

questions.subject: Ethics
questions.groupTitle: Elements of the Interhuman and a Phenomenology of Love
questions.prompt: Which action best applies the essays in a workplace disagreement?

choices.text: Address the actual person, supply relevant information, acknowledge disagreement, and allow a reply that can change the situation
Manage an image and reveal only facts that force compliance
Treat the colleague as a predictable role rather than a partner
Avoid opposition because confirmation requires approval

questions.explanation: Dialogue is truthful, answerable, and open to the other's agency.

distractorExplanations.b: ** B is manipulative seeming or propaganda.
distractorExplanations.c: ** C objectifies the person.
distractorExplanations.d: ** D confuses confirmation with agreement.

quizzes.title: Legal Aspects Part 1
quizzes.description: Questions 1–69 from the complete Legal Aspects pool.
quizzes.subject: Legal Aspects

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the lesson's definition and purpose of law?

choices.text: Rules based mainly on personal emotion and private preference
Rules established by recognized authority to regulate community life
Customs accepted by a group and enforced through social approval
Physical principles that describe motion, gravity, and acceleration

questions.explanation: Law is a set of rules established by a recognized authority to regulate how people live and interact within a community.

distractorExplanations.a: A confuses law with emotion, which the ordinance-of-reason idea rejects.
distractorExplanations.c: C describes non-legal social rules rather than state law.
distractorExplanations.d: D describes physical laws rather than legal rules.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: Under the St. Thomas Aquinas framework presented, which feature requires that a law be properly published or communicated?

choices.text: Ordinance of reason
Common good
Promulgation
State enforcement

questions.explanation: Promulgation means making the law known to the public so people can be expected to follow it.

distractorExplanations.a: A concerns rational rather than emotional lawmaking.
distractorExplanations.b: B concerns society-wide welfare rather than publication.
distractorExplanations.d: D describes state law generally, not this Aquinas element.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: Article 3 of the Civil Code means every Filipino must personally know the text of every law.
questions.explanation: The lesson says Article 3 does not require personal knowledge of every law; it prevents a person from avoiding liability merely by claiming ignorance after proper enactment and publication.
questions.correctedStatement: Once a law is properly enacted and published, ignorance does not excuse noncompliance.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: A hotel follows a faith-based practice that is recognized by its religious community but not enforced by the state. The lesson classifies the practice as which kind of rule?

choices.text: State law
Moral law
Divine law
Natural law

questions.explanation: Divine law is promulgated and enforced through religion and faith.

distractorExplanations.a: A is established and enforced by government authority.
distractorExplanations.b: B concerns social standards of right and wrong.
distractorExplanations.d: D concerns principles reason recognizes as inherently right or wrong.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: Which pairing is accurate under the lesson's categories of non-legal law?

choices.text: Moral law - gravity and inertia
Natural law - inherent right and wrong discerned by reason
Physical law - standards recognized by society
Divine law - rules enacted by the legislature

questions.explanation: Natural law refers to principles that human reason recognizes as inherently right or wrong.

distractorExplanations.a: A assigns physical examples to moral law.
distractorExplanations.c: C assigns moral standards to physical law.
distractorExplanations.d: D assigns state legislation to divine law.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: Article 1156 describes an obligation as a juridical necessity to do which of the following?

choices.text: Give, perform, or refrain from an act
Negotiate, perfect, or consummate a contract
Pay money, sign a writing, or register property
Demand, forgive, or replace an existing debt

questions.explanation: The three prestations are to give, to do, and not to do.

distractorExplanations.b: B lists stages of a contract from Lesson 5.
distractorExplanations.c: C narrows obligations to forms not stated in Article 1156.
distractorExplanations.d: D lists possible acts involving obligations but not the statutory definition.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: A juridical necessity is more than a moral promise because the law recognizes it and supplies remedies for nonperformance.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes an enforceable legal obligation from a merely personal promise.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: A resort agrees to deliver a specific shuttle van to a buyer. What kind of prestation is involved?

choices.text: To give
To do
Not to do
To refrain

questions.explanation: Delivering a thing is a prestation to give.

distractorExplanations.b: B requires performance of work or service.
distractorExplanations.c: C requires abstaining from a particular act.
distractorExplanations.d: D restates a negative prestation, not delivery.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: A chef is hired to prepare an anniversary dinner. Which prestation best describes the chef's duty?

choices.text: To give
To do
Not to do
To transfer a right

questions.explanation: Preparing the dinner is the performance of a service or work, so it is a prestation to do.

distractorExplanations.a: A centers on delivery of a thing.
distractorExplanations.c: C centers on refraining from an act.
distractorExplanations.d: D is not the classification used for this service.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: A hotel agrees not to disclose a guest's itinerary. Which prestation is created?

choices.text: To give
To do
Not to do
To pay

questions.explanation: The hotel must refrain from disclosure, which is a prestation not to do.

distractorExplanations.a: A requires delivery of a thing.
distractorExplanations.b: B requires affirmative service or work.
distractorExplanations.d: D is a monetary form of giving, not the agreed restraint.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: In the confirmed-room example, Maria Santos has the right to demand performance. What essential element does she represent?

choices.text: Passive subject
Juridical tie
Active subject
Prestation

questions.explanation: The active subject or creditor is the person entitled to demand performance.

distractorExplanations.a: A is the party bound to perform.
distractorExplanations.b: B is the legal bond between the parties.
distractorExplanations.d: D is the thing, act, or omission due.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: In that same confirmed-room example, the hotel is the passive subject because it has which role?

choices.text: The right to demand the room
The duty to provide the room
The act of confirming the room
The bond created by the booking

questions.explanation: The passive subject or debtor is the party bound to perform the obligation.

distractorExplanations.a: A belongs to the active subject.
distractorExplanations.c: C is an event showing agreement, not a subject.
distractorExplanations.d: D describes the juridical tie.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: What is the prestation in Maria Santos' confirmed booking?

choices.text: Maria Santos as the creditor
The hotel as the debtor
The confirmed legal relationship
Providing the Deluxe King Room on the agreed date

questions.explanation: The prestation is the specific thing, act, or omission that must be performed.

distractorExplanations.a: A identifies the active subject.
distractorExplanations.b: B identifies the passive subject.
distractorExplanations.c: C identifies the juridical tie.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: Which element gives an obligation its binding force by legally connecting creditor and debtor?

choices.text: Active subject
Passive subject
Prestation
Juridical tie

questions.explanation: The juridical tie, or vinculum juris, is the legal bond that binds the parties.

distractorExplanations.a: A is the party entitled to demand.
distractorExplanations.b: B is the party bound to perform.
distractorExplanations.c: C is the performance that is due.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Introduction to Law and Understanding Obligations
questions.prompt: The term creditor always refers to a person who lent money, and debtor always refers to a person who borrowed money.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses the terms more broadly: a creditor may demand any lawful prestation, and a debtor is any party bound to perform it.
questions.correctedStatement: Creditor and debtor refer to the right to demand and the duty to perform, not only to money loans.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: Which source of obligation is imposed directly by legislation, exists even without agreement, and is not presumed?

choices.text: Law
Contract
Quasi-contract
Quasi-delict

questions.explanation: An obligation arising from law is imposed directly by legislation and need not rest on consent.

distractorExplanations.b: B arises from the parties' meeting of minds.
distractorExplanations.c: C arises without agreement to prevent unjust enrichment.
distractorExplanations.d: D arises from negligent damage without intent.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: Two parties voluntarily agree on catering terms. The agreement has the force of law between them and must be performed in good faith. What is the source?

choices.text: Crime
Law
Contract
Quasi-contract

questions.explanation: A contract arises from the voluntary meeting of minds and binds the parties in good faith.

distractorExplanations.a: A involves an act or omission punished by law.
distractorExplanations.b: B is imposed directly by legislation.
distractorExplanations.d: D exists without an actual agreement.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: A hotel receives a payment that was not owed and must return it so it will not be unjustly enriched. Which source applies?

choices.text: Contract
Quasi-contract through solutio indebiti
Crime with civil liability
Quasi-delict through negligence

questions.explanation: Solutio indebiti is payment not due, a quasi-contractual situation requiring return of what was not owed.

distractorExplanations.a: A requires an agreement, which the facts lack.
distractorExplanations.c: C requires an offense causing compensable injury.
distractorExplanations.d: D requires negligent damage, not mistaken payment.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: Every crime necessarily creates civil liability against the offender, even when no one suffers compensable injury.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that some crimes produce no civil liability because no damage must be compensated.
questions.correctedStatement: Civil liability may arise from crime, but crimes such as treason, gambling, or illegal possession may involve no compensable damage.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: A driver carelessly damages a guest's luggage without intending the harm. Which source most directly applies?

choices.text: Law
Contract
Crime
Quasi-delict

questions.explanation: A quasi-delict involves negligence that causes damage without intent.

distractorExplanations.a: A is a duty directly imposed by legislation.
distractorExplanations.b: B depends on the breached agreement rather than the negligent act described.
distractorExplanations.c: C ordinarily involves an act or omission punished as an offense.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: Why does the lesson classify obligations?

choices.text: To determine demandability, manner of performance, and breach consequences
To decide whether every obligation must be written and notarized
To identify whether all obligations require the same prestation
To remove differences between legal and non-legal duties

questions.explanation: Classification explains when an obligation is demandable, how it must be performed, and what follows from breach.

distractorExplanations.b: B concerns contract form, not the stated purpose.
distractorExplanations.c: C contradicts the lesson that obligations differ.
distractorExplanations.d: D confuses legal classification with kinds of law.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: A borrower promises to repay P5,000 without attaching any future event. How is the obligation classified?

choices.text: Conditional
With a period
Pure
Facultative

questions.explanation: A pure obligation is immediately demandable because no condition or uncertain event must occur first.

distractorExplanations.a: A depends on a future uncertain event.
distractorExplanations.b: B becomes demandable upon a future certain event or date.
distractorExplanations.d: D has one principal prestation with an optional substitute.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: Payment for a wedding cake becomes due only if the client proceeds with the reception. What classification fits?

choices.text: Pure
Conditional
With a period
Divisible

questions.explanation: The obligation depends on a future event that may or may not happen.

distractorExplanations.a: A is immediately demandable without a condition.
distractorExplanations.c: C depends on an event certain to arrive.
distractorExplanations.d: D concerns whether performance can be divided.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: A balance must be paid ten days before the event. Why is this an obligation with a period rather than a conditional obligation?

choices.text: The due date is a future event certain to arrive
The event may or may not occur at the debtor's choice
The payment is immediately demandable without qualification
The debtor may substitute another prestation

questions.explanation: A period fixes when demandability arrives through a future certain date or event.

distractorExplanations.b: B describes a condition.
distractorExplanations.c: C describes a pure obligation.
distractorExplanations.d: D describes a facultative obligation.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: A restaurant agrees from the start that it may serve sea bass or tuna if salmon is unavailable, and either alternative satisfies the promise. What type is this?

choices.text: Facultative
Alternative
Joint
Conditional

questions.explanation: In an alternative obligation, two or more prestations are due and performance of one satisfies the obligation.

distractorExplanations.a: A has one original prestation and an optional substitute.
distractorExplanations.c: C concerns multiple debtors or creditors.
distractorExplanations.d: D concerns an uncertain event.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: A contract requires prestation A but permits B solely as a substitute if A cannot be performed. What type is this?

choices.text: Alternative
Solidary
Facultative
Indivisible

questions.explanation: A facultative obligation has one prestation originally due and another available only as a substitute.

distractorExplanations.a: A places multiple prestations in the obligation from the beginning.
distractorExplanations.b: B concerns liability for the whole debt.
distractorExplanations.d: D concerns performance as one complete act.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: When several debtors are involved, the obligation is generally presumed solidary unless the contract states otherwise.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that multiple-debtor obligations are generally presumed joint unless law or contract provides otherwise.
questions.correctedStatement: Each joint debtor ordinarily answers only for that debtor's share unless solidarity is established.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: Three cafe owners owe P300,000 jointly. One owner fails to pay. What may the supplier ordinarily demand from another owner?

choices.text: That owner's one-third share only
The entire P300,000 without qualification
One-half of the unpaid balance
Any amount chosen by the supplier

questions.explanation: Joint liability separates the debt into shares, so each debtor answers only for that debtor's portion.

distractorExplanations.b: B describes solidary liability.
distractorExplanations.c: C does not follow the three equal shares stated.
distractorExplanations.d: D ignores the defined limits of a joint share.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: Three restaurant partners expressly sign as solidary debtors. If the loan is unpaid, what may the bank do?

choices.text: Collect only equal shares from all three at once
Demand the entire obligation from any one partner
Collect only from the partner who managed the restaurant
Wait until each partner voluntarily identifies a share

questions.explanation: Under solidarity, the creditor may demand the entire obligation from any one debtor, subject to reimbursement among debtors.

distractorExplanations.a: A is the joint-liability approach.
distractorExplanations.c: C is not the criterion given in the lesson.
distractorExplanations.d: D would defeat the creditor's right under solidarity.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: Delivery of 1,000 bottles in four agreed weekly batches is best classified as what?

choices.text: Indivisible
Penal
Divisible
Facultative

questions.explanation: The obligation is divisible because partial performance in agreed batches is possible.

distractorExplanations.a: A requires one complete performance.
distractorExplanations.b: B adds a penalty for nonperformance.
distractorExplanations.d: D concerns an optional substitute.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: A private chef is hired to complete a seven-course tasting menu for one dinner but serves only three courses and leaves. Which feature makes the obligation indivisible?

choices.text: The menu can be paid in installments
Partial performance defeats the agreed purpose
The chef may choose any substitute menu
Several creditors share the right to demand

questions.explanation: The prestation must be completed as one whole because partial performance defeats the agreement's purpose.

distractorExplanations.a: A concerns payment structure, not the service's completeness.
distractorExplanations.c: C would describe facultative or alternative performance.
distractorExplanations.d: D concerns plurality of creditors, not divisibility.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sources and Classifications of Obligations
questions.prompt: A bakery must pay P5,000 for each unjustified delay in supplying pastries. What is the legal role of the P5,000 clause?

choices.text: It replaces the original supply obligation from the outset
It is an accessory consequence encouraging compliance

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sole Proprietorship Partnership and Corporation
questions.prompt: Which characteristic belongs to a corporation under the Revised Corporation Code?

choices.text: A natural person created by private agreement alone
An artificial being created by operation of law with succession and granted powers
A trade name that has no separate personality
A temporary association that ends whenever an owner changes

questions.explanation: A corporation is an artificial juridical person created by law, with succession and legally granted powers.

distractorExplanations.a: A denies its artificial and statutory nature.
distractorExplanations.c: C describes a sole-proprietor misconception.
distractorExplanations.d: D conflicts with succession.

questions.subject: Legal Aspects
questions.groupTitle: Sole Proprietorship Partnership and Corporation
questions.prompt: What does the doctrine of separate juridical personality mean for Bea Hospitality Ventures Inc?

choices.text: Bea and the corporation are legally identical
The corporation is separate and distinct from Bea and its stockholders
The corporation cannot own property in its own name
Every corporate debt is automatically Bea's personal debt

questions.explanation: The corporation is its own juridical person, able to own, contract, sue, and be sued.

distractorExplanations.a: A denies separation.
distractorExplanations.c: C denies a corporate power.
distractorExplanations.d: D contradicts the usual limited-liability effect.

When stockholders receive lawful dividends
When directors delegate work to officers

questions.prompt: Who manages the corporation according to the lesson?

choices.text: The proprietor acting alone
The partners under their agreement
The board of directors or trustees through corporate officers
Every creditor in proportion to the debt

questions.explanation: Corporate governance rests with the board or trustees and designated officers.

distractorExplanations.a: A describes sole proprietorship.
distractorExplanations.b: B describes partnership.
distractorExplanations.d: D creditors do not manage merely by lending.

questions.prompt: Which comparison between stock and nonstock corporations is accurate?

choices.text: Stock corporations divide capital into shares and may declare dividends; nonstock income serves its purposes without distributable dividends
Nonstock corporations have shares, while stock corporations have members only
Both must distribute all income annually
Neither has a separate juridical personality

questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes share capital and dividends from nonstock membership and purpose-directed income.

distractorExplanations.b: B reverses the terms.
distractorExplanations.c: C contradicts the nonstock rule.
distractorExplanations.d: D contradicts corporate personality.

questions.prompt: Which term refers to the persons who originally formed the corporation?

choices.text: Corporators
Incorporators
Stockholders
Members

questions.explanation: Incorporators are the original organizers; corporators is the broader class composing the entity.

distractorExplanations.a: A is broader.
distractorExplanations.c: C identifies owners in a stock corporation.
distractorExplanations.d: D identifies participants in a nonstock corporation.

questions.prompt: Why is a One Person Corporation not a sole proprietorship?

choices.text: It must have two or more partners
It keeps a separate juridical personality despite one stockholder
Its owner has unlimited liability by definition
It cannot enter contracts in its own name

questions.explanation: The OPC is still a corporation separate from its single stockholder.

distractorExplanations.a: A conflicts with one stockholder.
distractorExplanations.c: C ignores the corporate structure.
distractorExplanations.d: D denies corporate powers.
